title: Dominic and the Kitchen
premise: Paloma Voss, a single mother and owner of the town's only bookshop, agrees to a fake date with Dominic Reyes — the estranged heir who just inherited the failing vineyard next door — to survive her family's reunion without pitying looks. What begins as a transactional arrangement deepens as Dominic's harvest season and Paloma's daughter's custody questions force both to confront the identities they've been hiding behind: hers as the woman who fled, his as the son who was never wanted. When a letter reveals Dominic's inheritance came with conditions that could demolish the bookshop's lease, their fragile trust shatters at the worst possible moment. At the vineyard's first harvest festival, Paloma must forgive herself for the past she's punished herself over for fifteen years — and choose a future built not on safety, but on belonging.
about_author: Marguerite Blackwood is the pen name of a former sommelier turned bookseller who spent a decade in wine country before trading tasting notes for first drafts. She writes warm, slow-burn romances about people who inherit more than property.

chapters.title: The Last Bookshop on Alder Street
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. We meet Paloma closing up her bookshop, her daughter Wren doing homework in the reading nook, and the eviction-adjacent anxiety of a lease renewal letter she hasn't opened. Establishes her careful, measured life and the family reunion invitation she's dreading. Emotional beat: quiet dread beneath routine.

chapters.title: A Stranger Buys a Novel He'll Never Read
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic Reyes arrives in town to claim the vineyard he never wanted, wandering into the bookshop to escape his own name. He buys a novel on Paloma's recommendation purely to hear her talk about it. Emotional beat: two lonely people pretending to be fine.

chapters.title: Terms and Conditions of a Family Reunion
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Cornered by her sister's phone call demanding she bring 'someone,' Paloma impulsively proposes a fake date to Dominic when he returns to thank her for the recommendation. He hesitates, then agrees — he needs a reason to avoid his own family too. Emotional beat: reckless hope disguised as practicality.

chapters.title: Dessert Is Served
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The reunion: Paloma's relatives interrogate 'Dominic,' and the lie works too well — her grandmother blesses them, Wren beams, and by dessert the fake feels terrifyingly real. They leave separately but neither can stop smiling. Emotional beat: the crack where pretense becomes longing.

chapters.title: Vines and Other Living Things
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic surveys the neglected vineyard, discovering his grandfather's journals and realizing the harvest is six weeks away and the vines are dying. He asks Paloma — whose late father once worked these fields — for help. Emotional beat: grief for a legacy he rejected too soon.

chapters.title: What Wren Knows
chapters.summary: Wren's POV (first of two). Twelve-year-old Wren sees through the fake-dating ruse immediately but says nothing, cataloguing how her mother laughs differently around Dominic. A tender chapter about children protecting parents. Emotional beat: precocious heartbreak and hope.

chapters.title: The Reading Nook Rule
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Late-night inventory turns into wine on the shop floor; Dominic confesses he walked out at nineteen and never looked back, and Paloma almost tells him why she left town at twenty-two — but stops. First kiss, interrupted by a customer at the door. Emotional beat: intimacy outrunning honesty.

chapters.title: Harvest Hands
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Community volunteers arrive to save the vines, including Paloma's skeptical sister Marisol, who warns Dominic that Paloma breaks things off before they begin. Dominic learns fragments of Paloma's past from an old field hand. Emotional beat: falling for someone made of locked doors.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years Ago
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, flashback woven through present. We learn Paloma left town pregnant at twenty-two after being betrayed by her fiancé and disowned by half her family; the bookshop was her father's posthumous gift. She rehearses telling Dominic and fails. Emotional beat: shame calcified into identity.

chapters.title: A Letter in the Deed Box
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. In the estate lawyer's papers, Dominic finds a condition attached to his inheritance: the vineyard must turn a profit within one year, or the land — including the building housing Paloma's bookshop — reverts to a developer. He hides it. Emotional beat: love making a coward of him.

chapters.title: The Town That Raised Her
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A bookshop fundraiser doubles as a town celebration of the vineyard's revival; Paloma watches Dominic belong to this place in a way she never let herself. Wren calls him by his first name without prompting. Emotional beat: wanting what you've taught yourself not to need.

chapters.title: Marisol's Warning
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol confronts Paloma: she's seen the developer's surveyors near the vineyard and found the condition buried in public records. She gives Paloma twenty-four hours to hear it from Dominic instead. Emotional beat: protective fury and reluctant faith.

chapters.title: The Question She Shouldn't Have Asked
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma asks Dominic directly whether there's anything about the inheritance he hasn't told her. He lies — badly. She walks out mid-harvest-prep, taking Wren's hope with her. Emotional beat: old wounds confirming old beliefs.

chapters.title: Rain on the Trellises
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. A storm threatens the nearly ripe grapes days before harvest; Dominic works alone through the night, deciding that if he loses everything, he'll lose it honestly. He drafts a confession letter and a plan to buy the building himself. Emotional beat: choosing integrity over self-preservation.

chapters.title: Wren Runs
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Upset by the fighting, Wren skips school to visit the vineyard and is caught in the tail of the storm; Dominic finds her soaked and scared, and the two shelter in the cellar among his grandfather's barrels. He tells her the whole truth first. Emotional beat: trust rebuilt through a child's forgiveness.

chapters.title: Confession in the Cellar
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma arrives frantic, finds Wren safe, and overhears Dominic finishing his confession to Wren — including the part where he planned to tell Paloma everything and fix it himself. She realizes she asked him to be guilty of her ex-fiancé's sins. Emotional beat: the mirror moment — seeing her own fault clearly.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Woman in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Alone in the closed bookshop, Paloma finally grieves the fifteen years of self-punishment, reads her father's inscription inside her favorite novel — 'a home is a thing you allow' — and forgives herself. She opens the lease letter she'd been avoiding. Emotional beat: catharsis and resolve.

chapters.title: The Developer's Offer
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The developer makes a final play, offering Dominic a payout to walk away and let the condition default. Dominic refuses publicly at the town council meeting, revealing the condition himself and asking the community to help him meet the harvest quota. Emotional beat: a private man choosing transparency.

chapters.title: First Harvest
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, primarily Paloma. The whole town — Marisol, Wren, the field hands, the book club — turns out for the harvest. Paloma and Dominic work side by side, wordlessly repairing what broke. The tonnage comes in just over the threshold as the sun sets. Emotional beat: collective triumph, personal tenderness.

chapters.title: The Real Date
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic asks Paloma on a real date — same restaurant, no terms and conditions. Over dessert (deliberately), he offers her the bookshop's building at fair rent under a new long-term lease, co-signed as partners in every sense. She says yes to the date first, the lease second. Emotional beat: joy without armor.

chapters.title: Bottled and Labeled
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Months later: the first vintage is bottled, named 'Alder Street' after the bookshop; Wren designs the label. Paloma hosts the launch in the store, surrounded by the found family that formed around them. Her grandmother toasts 'the ones who stayed.' Emotional beat: belonging earned, not granted.

chapters.title: A Home Is a Thing You Allow
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, closing. One year later, Paloma locks up the bookshop and crosses the courtyard to the vineyard house where Wren and Dominic wait. She reflects that identity isn't what you fled or inherited, but what you build and permit yourself to keep. Final image: three names on the new sign. Emotional beat: peace, chosen daily.
